# Why the Second Batch of Sourdough Always Wins

First loaves are liars. Mine especially. The first attempt out of a new starter comes out dense, a little sour in the wrong way, crust like roofing material — and yet I always convince myself it's fine, actually, maybe even good? It is not good. It takes a second loaf, sometimes a third, before the starter settles into whatever rhythm it's going to keep for the rest of its life (assuming you don't kill it with tap water, which I have done, twice).

There's a woman at the farmers market who's been keeping the same culture alive for nineteen years. Nineteen. She feeds it on a schedule stricter than she keeps for herself, or so she claims, laughing, while she hands me a loaf still warm enough to fog the bag. I asked her once what happens if she goes on vacation. Fridge, she said. Slows it right down. Weeks, not days.

The chemistry is simple enough to explain and hard enough to feel, if that makes sense. Wild yeast and lactobacilli compete and cooperate in the same jar of flour paste, and depending on temperature, hydration, and how recently you fed it, you get more lactic acid (sharper, yogurt-like) or more acetic acid (vinegar, aggressive, sometimes unpleasant). Too acetic and the loaf tastes like it's punishing you.

I keep a log now — dumb as that sounds for bread — because the variables multiply fast: ambient temperature, flour brand, how long since the last feed, whether I stretched-and-folded four times or six. Four usually wins. Six overworks it, in my kitchen anyway, though I've read forum threads insisting the opposite, and who's to say their flour behaves like mine.

What nobody tells beginners is that the ear — that dramatic curling flap of crust from a good score — depends less on your blade technique than on whether the dough was properly proofed to begin with. Underproofed dough tears wrong no matter how sharp your lame is. Overproofed dough just sighs flat, no ear at all, no drama, a pancake with pretensions.

Second loaves win because by then you've corrected for whatever went wrong the first time: too wet, too cold, scored too late. It's not mystical. It's just that failure, here, is legible, and the oven doesn't lie to you twice in a row if you're paying attention.
